page6_img_fig5.png.title: Abstraction of literal values into named regex-derived AST nodes
page6_img_fig5.png.description: The figure illustrates binnacle’s abstraction step: the top-left lists example named regular expressions (e.g., ABS-URL-HTTPS → ^https://, ABS-URL-HTTP → ^http://, ABS-PATH-REL → ^(\.)+/, and a generic ABS-URL). The lower-left diagram shows a parse tree fragment before abstraction where a CURL-URL leaf contains the literal string "https://example.com." The lower-right diagram shows the result of abstraction: the CURL-URL node now has abstract child nodes (ABS-URL-HTTPS and ABS-URL) produced by matching the literal against the named regexes. This transformation removes raw literals and replaces them with typed abstract nodes that the miner and the enforcement engine can use to learn and check semantic rules (for example, enforcing HTTPS usage).

page8_img_3.png.title: M3: Fraction of EU leaves unresolved after Phase III parsing
page8_img_3.png.description: A density histogram of metric M3 showing the fraction of leaves that remained effectively uninterpretable (EU) after the third (Phase III) parsing pass. The distribution is tightly concentrated at zero (median 0.0%), with a very high density spike near 0% (note the broken y-axis to show this peak) and a long, low-density right tail extending toward larger percentages. The mean is 3.7%, and over 65% of trees had all previously-EU leaves resolved by Phase III, indicating that only a small fraction of files retain unresolved literal nodes after the top-50 command option parsing stage.

page8_img_2.png.title: Histogram of EU leaves after Phase II parsing (M2)
page8_img_2.png.description: A density histogram of the percentage of leaves in each Dockerfile that are classified as effectively uninterpretable (EU) after the second (embedded-bash) parsing phase. The x-axis is “% of EU leaves” and the y-axis is density; the paper reports a mean of 33.2% and median of 33.3% for M2. The bulk of files lie roughly in the ~20–50% range (the green shaded box marks the interquartile range), with a long right tail reaching toward 100%, illustrating that Phase II increases the proportion of literal/unknown leaf nodes compared to Phase I (mean 19.3%) and thus creates more unresolved structure that Phase III aims to recover.

page2_img_1.png.title: binnacle toolset architecture: collection, phased parsing, rule mining, and enforcement
page2_img_1.png.description: A three-stage pipeline diagram showing how binnacle ingests GitHub repositories, learns rules from expert Dockerfiles, and enforces those rules over a corpus. The top “Setup and Collect” stage applies query filters (Stars ≥ 10; created between 01-01-2007 and 06-01-2019) and a file-name filter ((d|D)ockerfile.*) to drive a Repository Ingestor and File Downloader that interact with GitHub and populate a Metadata Store and Dockerfile Corpus, while a Gold Set of official docker-library files is identified. The middle “Learn Rules” stage feeds the Gold Set through the Phased Parser and a Rule Miner to produce a Mined Rules store. The bottom “Enforce Rules” stage parses the full Dockerfile Corpus with the Phased Parser and applies the Rule Enforcement Engine (using the learned/manual Rules) to produce a Rule Violations output.

page5_img_fig_1.png.title: Three example Tree Association Rules (TARs) for Dockerfile patterns
page5_img_fig_1.png.description: The figure shows three example Tree Association Rules encoded as S‑expressions and labeled with their location relation: "Precedes", "Follows", and "Child-Of". (a) The Precedes rule has (APT-GET-INSTALL) above the bar and (APT-GET-UPDATE) below, expressing that an apt-get install should be preceded (in the same Dockerfile layer) by an apt-get update. (b) The Follows rule uses (APT-GET-INSTALL) as the antecedent and a consequent expressed as (RM (RM-F-RECURSIVE) (RM-PATH (ABS-APT-LISTS))) to indicate that a recursive rm of the apt lists directory should follow an install. (c) The Child-Of rule binds a region inside (APT-GET-INSTALL [*]) and requires a (FLAG-NO-RECOMMENDS) child, illustrating intra-tree (child) constraints and the use of the [*] marker for where to search for the consequent.

page8_img_1.png.title: Density of % of effectively uninterpretable (EU) leaves after Phase I parsing
page8_img_1.png.description: A density histogram (x-axis: % of EU leaves, y-axis: density) showing the distribution of M1 — the fraction of leaves marked effectively uninterpretable after the top-level (Phase I) parse. The plot reports an average of 19.3% and a median of 16.7% EU leaves; the green shaded box marks the interquartile range (the middle 50% of the data). The distribution is right-skewed with most of the density concentrated at low percentages (most files under ~40% EU leaves) and a long tail reaching up to 100%, indicating a small number of files with very high fractions of EU leaves.

page6_img_fig4.png.title: Rule-mining example: frequent sub-trees from APT-GET-INSTALL and derived TARs
page6_img_fig4.png.description: The figure visualizes binnacle’s frequent sub-tree rule-mining workflow using APT-GET-INSTALL subtrees. Panel (a) shows four concrete subtree instances rooted at APT-GET-INSTALL with child nodes such as FLAG-YES, FLAG-QUIET, PACKAGES and package leaves (examples: python3, mysql, nginx, gcc, make). Panel (b) highlights two frequently occurring subtrees (gray and dashed outlines) extracted by a frequent-sub-tree miner (CMTreeMiner) with a 75% support threshold. Panel (c) shows the resulting Tree Association Rules (TARs): the antecedent is the APT-GET-INSTALL root (with an optional [*] binding) and the mined consequents include patterns like FLAG-NO-RECOMMENDS and the subtree (FLAG-YES) (PACKAGES (PACKAGE)).

page4_img_1.png.title: Phased parsing of a Dockerfile into enriched AST nodes
page4_img_1.png.description: The figure shows an example Dockerfile (FROM ubuntu:latest; RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -qqy ...; RUN ./scripts/custom.sh) and the corresponding AST at three parsing phases. Phase I (top-level parse) represents embedded shell fragments as string literal leaves (shaded gray) that are effectively uninterpretable (EU). Phase II parses the embedded bash, exposing a BASH-AND node with two BASH-COMMAND children (one for apt-get update and one for apt-get install -qqy ...), but still leaves some literals unresolved. Phase III further parses popular command invocations (the top-50 commands), turning the apt-get install literal into structured nodes (APT-GET-INSTALL with FLAG-YES, FLAG-QUIET, and a PACKAGES/PACKAGE subtree) and the apt-get update into APT-GET-UPDATE, while the external ./scripts/custom.sh remains an UNKNOWN leaf; this illustrates how phased parsing progressively converts EU leaves into semantically richer AST nodes (the paper reports over an 80% reduction in EU nodes corpus-wide).

page7_img_1.png.title: Parsed Dockerfile AST with matched APT‑GET‑INSTALL subtree
page7_img_1.png.description: A tree diagram of a parsed Dockerfile showing the AST nodes produced by phased parsing. The root is DOCKER-FILE with three children: a DOCKER-FROM node (with leaves ubuntu and latest) and two DOCKER-RUN nodes. The first DOCKER-RUN contains a BASH-AND node whose children are three BASH-COMMAND subtrees: APT-GET-UPDATE, an APT-GET-INSTALL subtree (outlined in bold to indicate it matches a rule antecedent), and MAKE; the APT-GET-INSTALL subtree further decomposes into FLAG-YES, FLAG-QUIET (with a literal '2' shown), and a PACKAGES→PACKAGE list (ellipsis). The second DOCKER-RUN contains a BASH-COMMAND with an UNKNOWN leaf. The figure illustrates Stage I of binnacle’s enforcement process: locating a rule antecedent (the apt-get-install subtree) in the enriched AST so the engine can subsequently check the appropriate region for the required consequent (e.g., an apt-get-update).

page5_img_table_1.png.title: Gold Rules breakdown: rule names, consequences, support, and confidence
page5_img_table_1.png.description: The figure is a table of 23 candidate Dockerfile rules with columns for Rule Name, whether the rule is a Bash best-practice, Immediate Violation Consequences, Future Violation Consequences, Gold Set Support (count), and Gold Set Confidence (percentage). Fifteen rows are shaded (the 15 Gold Rules that passed quantitative filtering); support values in the table range widely (from single digits up to 632) and confidence values range from 46.67% to 100%, with many rules above 90% (for example, aptGetUpdatePrecedesInstall, aptGetInstallUseY, and aptGetInstallRmAptLists each have support 525 and 100% confidence). The Immediate Violation Consequences column frequently lists “Space wastage” or “Build failure,” while Future Violation Consequences often list “Increased attack surface” or “Build reliability” issues; the Bash Best-practice? column marks which rules encode general shell best-practices versus Docker-specific patterns.

page7_img_3.png.title: Dockerfile AST showing antecedent match with one consequent present and one missing
page7_img_3.png.description: A parsed AST of a Dockerfile with colored regions illustrating binnacle’s rule-enforcement Stage III. The APT-GET-INSTALL node is emphasized with a thick black outline as the matched antecedent; a blue shaded region (labeled 2) bound as the ‘‘preceding/intra-directive’’ area contains a dashed black APT-GET-UPDATE subtree (indicating that this required consequent is present). A green shaded region (labeled 3) bound as the ‘‘child-of’’ area shows an expected FLAG-NO-RECOMMENDS consequent drawn as a dashed red box but not found among the actual children (which include FLAG-YES, FLAG-QUIET, and PACKAGES), indicating a rule violation. The figure therefore demonstrates how the engine locates an antecedent, binds the appropriate region, and then validates or reports a missing consequent.

page9_img_1.png.title: Four example Tree Association Rules (APK, curl-HTTPS, cp paths, sed in-place)
page9_img_1.png.description: A horizontal sequence of four small rule diagrams, each labeled with the location "Child-Of" and showing an antecedent subtree (root node with a [*] binder) above a horizontal bar and a consequent subtree below. From left to right: (a) antecedent (APK-ADD [*]) with consequent (FLAG-NO-CACHE) — a Gold rule that encodes using apk add with the --no-cache flag; (b) antecedent (SC-CURL-URL [*]) with consequent (ABS-URL-PROTOCOL-HTTPS) — a semantic rule requiring curl URLs use HTTPS; (c) antecedent (CP [*]) with consequent showing two CP-PATH children — a syntactic rule capturing that cp takes two path arguments; and (d) antecedent (SED [*]) with consequent (FLAG-IN-PLACE) — an ungeneralizable mined rule asserting sed is used with an in‑place flag. These exemplify the kinds of TARs the paper’s miner recovers: safety/quality best-practices (a,b), basic structural constraints (c), and rules that may be correct on the corpus but unlikely to generalize (d).

page7_img_2.png.title: Dockerfile AST with numbered bound regions for TAR rule enforcement
page7_img_2.png.description: A tree-shaped AST rooted at DOCKER-FILE shows a central DOCKER-RUN that sequences bash commands; the antecedent subtree APT-GET-INSTALL is outlined in black. Five colored, numbered binding regions illustrate where the enforcement engine will look for a rule’s consequent: region 2 (blue, intra-directive preceding) contains an APT-GET-UPDATE command, region 3 (green, child-of) contains FLAG-YES, FLAG-QUIET and PACKAGES/ PACKAGE children under the install, and region 5 (red, intra-directive following) contains a MAKE command; regions 1 and 4 (darker blue/red) are the inter-directive counterparts (e.g., a DOCKER-FROM ubuntu:latest and an UNKNOWN command). The diagram visualizes Stage II of binnacle’s enforcement: after matching the antecedent (APT-GET-INSTALL), the engine binds one of these numbered regions (depending on rule location/scope) and then searches that region for the consequent subtree.
